title: Learning Lotteries with Minimal Stakeholder Violations from Membership Queries
claim: Acceptable sets are halfspace slices of the probability simplex, and a few queried agents can leave unqueried agents' preferences unconstrained.
layout: 2 panels, side-by-side triangles, labeled simplex corners, shaded strip and highlighted edge
description: Two side-by-side triangles represent the probability simplex over three alternatives, with corners labeled e1 (bottom left), e2 (bottom right) and e3 (top). Panel (a) shows a halfspace acceptance region A_i as a shaded blue area cut by a diagonal line. A lighter inner region marks the lotteries the agent accepts, and a darker strip next to the boundary marks the margin band of width eta. Panel (b) shows the lower-bound construction. A thick dark-red segment runs along the bottom edge from e1 to e2, with a larger red dot at e1. A single black dot labeled x-hat sits inside the triangle. The eye goes first to the blue strip in (a) and the red edge in (b). Captions (a) and (b) sit below each triangle.
caption: Lotteries over three alternatives drawn as points of a triangle with corners $\be_1,\be_2,\be_3$. (a) An agent's acceptable set $A_i$ (shaded) is the part of the triangle on one side of a line; the darker strip contains the lotteries that the agent accepts with margin less than $\eta$. (b) The profile in the proof of Theorem [ref] when $\widehat\bx\neq\be_1$: every queried agent accepts exactly the lotteries on the bottom edge, and every unqueried agent accepts only $\be_1$. All unqueried agents reject $\widehat\bx$, but every agent accepts $\be_1$.
abstract: An AI developer often has several candidate versions of a system and can deploy a mixture of them, sending each request to a randomly chosen version, as in A/B testing. Each stakeholder (e.g., a safety team, a regulator, or a customer with private test data) accepts a mixture exactly when its expected performance (e.g., its rate of harmful replies) meets the stakeholder's own standard, which the developer can learn only by asking whether a proposed mixture is acceptable. We model this as choosing a lottery over $m$ alternatives for $n$ agents, each of whom accepts exactly the lotteries in an unknown halfspace and answers such binary membership queries. While Choo et al. (ICML 2026) sought a lottery that every agent accepts, none may exist when, say, safety and helpfulness requirements conflict, so we minimize the number of rejecting agents. We show that this problem is APX-hard even when all halfspaces are known and all utilities are $0$ or $1$. We then give exact algorithms that run in polynomial time when $m$ is constant, and in quasi-polynomial time when, for a constant $Î·$, some optimal lottery has no accepting agent within $Î·$ of its threshold. When only some agents can be queried, optimizing over a uniform sample of agents gives additive and relative guarantees for the whole population, with a sample size that does not depend on $n$, and a linear program gives a polynomial-time method for any $m$. On the other hand, for $m\ge 3$, a deterministic algorithm that queries only $K$ distinct agents cannot guarantee fewer than $n-K$ extra rejections, and this is achievable; in other words, it can guarantee nothing for the agents it does not ask. Small synthetic experiments indicate that our worst-case bounds are conservative on random instances.
